Exhaustive search with latency-preserving input-variable permutation reduction establishes a minimum latency of 126.745ps over all 5-bit APN permutations under the prescribed gate-delay model, with explicit constructions attaining this minimum in every class.The classification results give the optimized latency distributions and numbers of optimal IP classes of input-affine transformations within each affine class. Comparisons with selected 5-bit S-box implementations under the same model show simultaneous reductions in some cases: latency decreases by $10.20\%$--$29.18\%$ and normalized gate area by $5.37\%$--$27.69\%$, while preserving the original S-box mappings.

item.title: Revisiting Accountability in Accountable Tracing Signatures
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2718
Authors: Rei Naito, Kyoichi Asano, Keita Emura
Summary: Accountable tracing signatures (ATS), introduced by Kohlweiss and Miers (PoPETs 2015), classify each group member (user) as either traceable or non-traceable. A traceable user corresponds to one in conventional group signature schemes whose identity can be revealed by the opener from a signature, whereas a non-traceable user cannot be identified from any signature they produce. The opener, who issues a witness, can certify a user's status via the Account algorithm. In this paper, we formalize accountability soundness, which ensures that no two witnesses can simultaneously certify a user as both traceable and non-traceable. We show that the Kohlweiss-Miers ATS scheme admits conflicting witnesses that violate this property. Since accountability is a fundamental aspect of ATS, as reflected in its name, such conflicting witnesses undermine the intended guarantees of the primitive. To address this issue, we propose a patched version of the Kohlweiss-Miers ATS scheme that provides accountability soundness. We also discuss the applicability of our attack to the lattice-based ATS scheme (Ling et al., CT-RSA 2019) and the isogeny-based ATS scheme (Shaw-Dutta, Indocrypt 2021), together with preliminary investigations of possible countermeasures. We emphasize that all our attacks fall outside the original security models.

item.title: Verifiable Data on Bitcoin: FlatMerkle Commitments, Refutable Proofs, and FlatChecks
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2717
Authors: Sergio Demian Lerner
Summary: We give a method to publish data on Bitcoin and to verify properties of that data on Bitcoin itself, against a publisher who may lie. The data is a FlatMerkle file – a structured byte string whose ordinary SHA-256 supports logarithmic inclusion proofs and logarithmic proofs of malformation – placed in a transaction's annex or, at four times the cost but relayable by Bitcoin Core, in an output. We show that the publisher's ordinary Taproot signature, with a suitably chosen signature-hash type, binds the publisher to the published data in a form that a dispute can authenticate with a single SHA-256 compression plus the signature check, or with three compressions when no annex is used. Claims about the data, and claims about such claims, are published as proof messages in two formats: a plain encoding, refuted by revealing it whole, and a traced encoding that stores the verifier's output after each level, so that any false message is refuted by revealing at most five of its elements. The format, chosen by a cost model that weighs challenge bytes against published bytes, is fixed by public context so that no message can be read in two formats; chains of claims about claims settle at four logical elements. A dispute thus reduces to a few dozen SHA-256 compressions and one Schnorr verification per commitment – too large for Bitcoin Script, but small enough to adjudicate with an interactive bisection game, a chunked script in the manner of BitVM2, or a garbled circuit. The same technique verifies any locally refutable verifier, one whose every rejection is witnessed by a single check over a few words of a canonical trace. In a FlatCheck, the prover publishes only the proof; the trace, the verifier's intermediate values, is published only if a challenger asks for it, and the dispute then examines the single check he names. When the verifier splits into groups that each read a few parts of the proof, a challenge forces the trace of one group only. We give two examples: a toy L2 of signed transfers, whose 512-transfer batches cost 12,200 vbytes to claim, and a Bitcoin header-chain light client verified on Bitcoin itself, which claims a retarget period of 2,016 headers in 45,200 vbytes; a dispute over a local check costs about 37,500 and 49,200 vbytes, and one over a malformed trace about 77,100 and 99,800, independently of the number of groups. Verifying STARK proofs is another application. We also remove FlatMerkle's restriction to power-of-two sizes without padding.

item.title: Key Recovery Against RLCE via the GIJS Distinguisher
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2716
Authors: Jacob Alperin-Sheriff
Summary: We present an experimental cryptanalysis of the RLCE cryptosystem at the heretofore secure $w=n-k$ parameter regime. Our attack relies crucially on the recent Ghoshal--Ishai--Jain--Sun (GIJS) distinguisher The attack shortens the public key at random positions, runs the GIJS distinguisher with \emph{every} column as hold-out, and uses this distinguisher to identify twin pairs based on how they appear across trials. Three pairs so identified are unmixed by a root-finding cascade, and Sidelnikov--Shestakov on the resulting $k \times (k+3)$ pure matrix recovers the key.
We experimentally verify our attack by breaking the ID-0 (128-bit) in 30.5 core-hours (about 3 hours of wall time) on a standard higher-end laptop.

item.title: A Constant-Rate Compiler for Continual Memory Leakage
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2715
Authors: Shweta Agrawal, Anuja Modi, Rajeev Raghunath
Summary: Leakage-resilient compilers transform any computation so that physical leakage from its implementation reveals nothing beyond its input-output behaviour. In this work, we investigate this question in the well-motivated continual memory leakage (CML) model, that captures a variety of relevant real-world side-channel attacks and subsumes several other well studied models in the leakage domain. In this model with two independently leaking components (at least two are necessary), all known general compilers tolerate only an inverse-polynomial leakage-rate.
We give a compiler with constant leakage-rate, in the hybrid model with a simple inputless leak-free sampler as in Dziembowski and Faust (TCC 2012). It protects any deterministic computation on a fixed secret with public inputs and outputs, and comes with a transfer theorem: any security game in which the adversary has an oracle for the computation remains secure when every oracle call is replaced by a compiled evaluation that leaks continuously. Our compiler uses no computational assumption.
Our main application is public-key encryption. Applied to the decryption of any IND-CCA2 secure PKE, the compiler gives IND-CCLA2 security, i.e. CCA2 security even when every decryption leaks, including after the challenge ciphertext, with the same public key, ciphertexts and encryption algorithm. Instantiating the base scheme gives such PKE from LWE and from LPN improving upon the previous best post-quantum constructions in this model, which supported only inverse-polynomial leakage-rate. We also obtain signatures, PRFs and MACs with constant leakage-rate via a natural generalization.
Our key idea is to pack the entire configuration of a universal machine into one element of a large extension field, so that any computation keeps only a constant number of inner-product encodings in memory at any time, each for only a constant number of rounds. Our techniques are inspired by packing techniques in homomorphic encryption adapted to a completely different context. We are optimistic that our techniques will find other applications.

item.title: Polynomial Batch Accumulators for Onboarding-Dominant Zero-Knowledge Membership Proofs
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2714
Authors: Samanta Karmaker, Sampad Sikder, Md Ariful Islam, Md Sadek Ferdous
Summary: Zero-knowledge membership accumulators are conventionally tailored for slowly growing sets with frequent proof generation, creating severe efficiency bottlenecks for modern compliance architectures. Governance-driven applications like FATF customer due diligence, eIDAS 2.0 wallet issuance, and MiCA VASP authorization invert this structure. In this regime, rosters are ingested at an enterprise scale, while proofs are requested selectively. To resolve this mismatch, we introduce Polynomial Equation Batching (PEB), a membership accumulator for onboarding heavy workloads. PEB represents up to 128 members per batch as a characteristic polynomial and hashes its coefficients via Poseidon, seamlessly scaling to arbitrarily large populations through parallel batching. We present two variants: PEB-A, which maps member secrets directly to polynomial roots for maximum performance, and PEB-B, which hashes secrets in-circuit for hardened security. Implemented in Noir and Barretenberg on BN254, and evaluated for up to 1,048,576 members, PEB provides significant performance improvements. Compared to incremental Merkle trees, PEB-A achieves up to a 149.07x mean speedup in per-user initialization while incurring a modest 33.87% proof-generation overhead. Additionally, against static Merkle trees, PEB-A delivers a 15.71x speedup during setup. By shifting off-circuit overhead from hash evaluations to field multiplications, PEB provides a highly efficient, scalable solution for real-world zero-knowledge compliance systems.

item.title: CHAMPing at the Bit: Short Square-Root Collisions for Two-Generator Cayley Hashes
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2713
Authors: Freeman Slaughter
Summary: For $A,B\in\text{GL}(\mathbb{F}_p)$, a Cayley hash $\text{HM}(w)$ maps a bit string $w \in \{0,1\}$ to the corresponding product of $A$ and $B$. We construct collisions by finding two palindromes whose matrix products commute. A symmetric form shared by the two generators places the hash of every palindrome in a three-dimensional subspace containing the identity. Two such hashes commute when their traceless parts are proportional, which defines a class map with $p+2$ values, so the pigeonhole principle gives collisions of $4\lceil\log_2(p+3)\rceil$ bits. Under a uniformity heuristic, a dictionary search finds such a pair after about $\sqrt{\pi p/2}$ class evaluations. Adding one bit to each half-message gives an expected bound of $O(\sqrt p)$ evaluations, with no assumption on how the classes are distributed. When the common form is singular, the generators are simultaneously triangular and the same argument applies to ordinary words.
For CHAMP-512 and CHAMP-1024, the heuristic search finds collisions of $512$ and $1024$ bits after about $2^{64}$ and $2^{128}$ class evaluations, and the one-bit-longer, distribution-independent variant finds collisions of $516$ and $1028$ bits at the same leading cost. This matches the asymptotic cost of an earlier commuting-product search for CHAMP, whose messages have $O(\log^2(p))$ bits, and improves on the bound of about $p$ given by an earlier palindrome restriction. For every pair over an odd prime field, this also shortens the collisions of the general algorithm of Mullan and Tsaban from $O(\log^2(p)/\log(\log(p)))$ to $4 \lceil \log_2(p+3) \rceil$ bits. Since the argument applies to every pair $A,B$, no pair of generators gives a $2\times2$ Cayley hash over $\mathbb{F}_p$ with collision resistance greater than $O(\sqrt p)$. We give an explicit proof-of-concept collision for the CHAMP matrices at a $36$-bit prime, and prove that every sufficiently short message can be recovered from its digest for the main CHAMP pair. To close, we demonstrate that since reversal and symbol exchange act as sign changes on quaternion coordinates, the alternative CHAMP pair possesses a much greater degree of symmetry, but do not yet see how to utilize this to find collisions below the square-root bound.

item.title: Concrete Minimum Distance Bounds of Accumulate Codes over any Fixed Finite Field
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2712
Authors: Alexander R. Block, Himanshu Dongre, Hendrik Waldner
Summary: We present a new concrete unified distance analysis of three accumulate-type error-correcting codes over any finite field, specifically the Repeat-Accumulate (RA), Repeat-Accumulate-Accumulate (RAA), and Expand-Accumulate (EA) codes. For message length $k$, codeword length $n$, finite field size $q>2$, and target relative minimum distance $\delta$, we give new upper bounds on the probability that each of the above codes do not have minimum distance at least $\delta$. Our bounds are concrete and explicit: they do not rely on $n$ or $q$ being sufficiently large. We present (multiple) closed-form upper bounds on the failure probability for each code, and complement these bounds with asymptotic analyses that (nearly) match prior-known asymptotic bounds. Our technical core is a new fine-grained union bound for accumulate codes, which may be of independent interest, that examines inputs to the accumulator from a purely distributional perspective, deriving properties that are necessary for an input vector to accumulate to a targeted output weight, and analyzing the probability the input distribution achieves these properties. This fine-grained union bound generalizes the input-output weight enumerator approach used by many prior works.
Our concrete analysis shows that (1) the RA code has concretely small distance (a maximum of $\delta\leq 2.4979\times10^{-8}$ for $k=2^{40}$ and $q=2^{32}$, except with probability $2^{-60}$), and (2) the RAA and EA codes achieve somewhat large concrete distance for smaller field sizes $q \leq 2^{32}$. Concretely, for rate $k/n = 1/4$, $k\in\{2^{40},2^{50}\}$, and $q=2^{8}$, the RAA code has distance $\delta=1/8$ except with $2^{-60}$ probability, whereas the rate $1/2$ and $1/4$ EA code for the same $k$ and $q=2^{4}$, respectively, has distance $\delta\leq 0.0689756$ and $\delta \leq0.232955$ except with probability $2^{-60}$. For fields of size $q\geq 2^{32}$, under our concrete bounds, all codes experience a sharp drop-off in attainable minimum distance, as our analysis targets (small) fixed $q$.

item.title: Fast Provable Algorithms for Approximate CVP and Exact SVP on Random \(q\)-ary Lattices
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2711
Authors: Jiseung Kim, Junhyuk Kwon, Changmin Lee, JeongHwan Lee
Summary: We give provable randomized algorithms for the $\gamma$-approximate Closest Vector Problem ($\gamma$-CVP) with $\gamma=5/3$ and the exact Shortest Vector Problem (SVP) in the Euclidean norm on random $q$-ary lattices. These lattices consist of the integer vectors mapped to zero modulo $q$ by a uniformly random matrix $\mathbf{H}\in(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^{m\times n}$, for any integer $q\ge2$. For input density $\delta=m\log_2q/n$ with $0\le\delta\le1$, the running times are $2^{0.2668n+o(n)}$ for $5/3$-CVP and $2^{0.2741n+o(n)}$ for exact SVP, with polynomial input-length factors suppressed. For $1<\delta\le3/2$, the respective bounds are $2^{0.56n+o(n)}$ and $2^{0.468n+o(n)}$. For all but a negligible fraction of matrices, both algorithms succeed with overwhelming probability over their internal randomness. Notably, for $0\le\delta\le1$, our provable bounds fall below even the $2^{0.2925n+o(n)}$ heuristic estimate for classical lattice sieving.
As a cryptographic application, we prove that signatures in the original construction of Gentry, Peikert, and Vaikuntanathan (GPV) can be forged in time $2^{0.0534n+o(n)}$ for $n\ge5m\log_2q$. For a $128$-bit security target, a leading-term estimate gives $n\approx2400$ and a public key of roughly $144$ kB, indicating a substantial storage burden.

item.title: Hidden Curves and Short Duals: Cubic Jets, Dual Leaks, and the Limits of Masked-Code Encryption
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2710
Authors: Yongge Wang
Summary: Masked-code encryption hides a decodable code behind a transformation meant to make it look random. We study the two masks proposed as compact alternatives to Goppa codes---Wang's RLCE and the $(U\,|\,U{+}V)$ construction of UVW-KEM---over the decodable hidden codes they have been or could be applied to, and find that, among the families examined, none yields a compact trapdoor.
Over Reed--Solomon and algebraic-geometry codes the mask hides a \emph{curve}, and curves are not hidden from jets. We explain the October 2026 key recovery of UVW-KEM (NGCC) and show it is not specific to UVW: for \emph{hidden-pairing codes} we bound from below the dependencies among order-$r$ jets of degree-$d$ forms at the columns of any shortening---for cubics $2k_1-k_2-k_l+2$ (UVW) and $2(n{-}k)-w-k_l+2$ (RLCE), attained in every regime tested, and we prove that the structured part of the dependency space carries the pairing and the secret ratios in closed form. Every proposed UVW parameter set has the predicted cubic deficiency (key recovery has been demonstrated at UVW-KEM-128). RLCE's long-key regime $w\ge n-k$, out of reach of the square-code attack for eight years, falls at degree three: on a full-size Level-1 parameter set we recover an equivalent key from the public key alone and decrypt fresh ciphertexts. HermitianRLCE is distinguished the same way. A forcing law, a master count and a redundancy law make the \emph{jet degree} an invariant of hidden-pairing codes: within that model, each unit of structural depth costs a unit of redundancy.
Without a curve the masks fail differently: both \emph{preserve the dual} of the hidden code, at most doubling the weight of every dual word. polarRLCE at rate $\le2/3$ leaks dual words found in $47$--$94$ bits; at higher rates no certified decoding radius supports $143$-bit security up to length $16384$, and at $32768$ the key is $58$\,MiB, $234\times$ Classic McEliece. LDPC codes leak their sparse checks, MDPC codes are better left unmasked, and UVW carries a matched-pair subspace for every hidden code. Reed--Muller-heavy codes under RLCE resist every attack here at $4$\,MiB keys, but only if a decoder at $3.4\times$ the bounded-distance radius exists.

item.title: Private Accounts Without $O(N)$ Work Through a Hybrid State Model
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2709
Authors: Philipp Gackstatter, François Garillot, Marti Górny, Adrian Hamelink, Al Kindi, Philippe Laferrière, Robin Salen, Brian Seong, Bobbin Threadbare
Summary: Privacy-preserving smart contracts face a scalability problem. In account-balance-vector designs, hiding which accounts changed requires that every transaction perform an indistinguishable update over the global state, so validators pay work linear in the number of accounts for every private transfer. UTXO systems avoid this by validating local spends, but do not provide the same account-style programming model.
We argue that the usual "account vs.~UTXO" framing conflates state representation and execution model, two choices that can be made separately. Miden, an Ethereum Layer 2, separates them. It uses persistent accounts for programmability, asynchronous notes for value transfer, and client-side proving for execution. Validators verify proofs and update commitments without re-executing transactions or accessing uninvolved state.
The result is an account-based platform with private transfers and private computation, while keeping validator work per transaction logarithmic in the number of accounts.
